text: Lesson eighty-five, Window Frames: ROWS versus RANGE. Chapter ten, Window and Ranking Functions.

Last lesson's LAST_VALUE gotcha came down to one thing: the frame. The frame clause controls exactly which rows within the current partition are included in the window function's calculation, relative to the current row. Both ROWS and RANGE share the same boundary vocabulary: unbounded preceding for the start of the partition, N preceding or following for a fixed distance, current row for the row itself, and unbounded following for the end of the partition. A frame is always written as between a start and an end.

ROWS counts physical rows. Sum of total due, over order by order date, rows between 2 preceding and current row, as sum of last 3 rows. That's always exactly three physical rows — the two immediately before the current one, plus the current row itself — regardless of what values they actually contain.

RANGE works differently. It counts by the LOGICAL value in the order by column instead of physical position. Range between current row and current row means every row whose order date EQUALS the current row's order date. If three different orders share the exact same date, all three are peers, and RANGE includes all of them together — not just the single current row. That's the surprise RANGE springs on people: it treats tied rows as a group.

This is exactly why the default LAST_VALUE frame misbehaved last lesson — it uses RANGE, which only looks up to the current row's logical position. As a rule: reach for ROWS almost all the time, since it's predictable and it's what running totals and moving averages are built from. Reach for RANGE only when you specifically want tied order-by values treated as one group.
Next lesson: Running Totals and Moving Averages — putting everything from this chapter together into the real payoff. See you there.
